translation: She looks at a family, all girls, a mother with a baby in her arms clumsily steps down from the cart and the driver is hurrying her because the cart must return to pick up others in the suburbs.
Her bag falls from her back, spilling contents that are some faded rags and a single string of small, darkened beads.
The woman gathers them embarrassedly as if she just revealed her most inaccessible secrets to the world.
Deymow passes her and suddenly a boy runs up to her, maybe six or seven years old.
Looking at her with smiling eyes and very pleased with himself he says: "Praise be Jesus Christ!".
She responds automatically but also solemnly: "Forever and ever amen.
Then she has heartache and tears well up in her eyes.
She squats near the boy grabbing his wrists while he continues looking directly into those tear-filled eyes still smiling like a little rascal.
The first buildings spring up before them unexpectedly, without warning.
It seems the fog alters the sense of distance because Kaśka herself even seems surprised by this.
Suddenly she jumps, jerking at the shafts and, if not for Roszek's firm reaction and his whip, would have overturned the cart.
Perhaps Kaska was frightened by sparks flying from the forge or maybe she sensed anxiety in horses waiting for their turn to be shod.
Everywhere one could smell the nauseating odor of malt that pervaded every commodity available for sale.
It was as nourishing as bread.
In the outskirts of Rohatyn, in Babince, there are a few small breweries which are responsible for spreading this saturating scent all around the area.
Many small shops sell beer here, and better stores have both vodka and mead, mainly three-year-old ones.
The stock in Jewish merchant Wakszul's store offers wine genuine Hungarian wine and true
Riesling as well as some slightly sour ones brought all the way from Wallachia.
The most could be said about the Wołowski family, as it had grown to vast proportions.
Nearly all branches of this family were ennobled, some bearing the Bawół coat of arms, others the Na Kaskach.
Without doubt an impressive career was made by Franciszek, son of Izaak Wołowski, who priest Chmielowski called Jeremiasz.
Born in 1786 in Brünn and raised in Offenbach, he became one of the best lawyers and law experts at that time.

Interestingly enough when there was a proposal in parliament to grant Polish citizenship to Jews, Franciszek as an MP argued persuasively in his riveting speech that it was not yet time for such a step.
First, the Polish nation must fight for independence and afterwards there would be time for social reforms.
All the neophytes of Offenbach were buried in the city cemetery, which after years became an obstacle to the city expansion plans and was closed down in 1866.
The remains of people buried there were collected and respectfully reburied elsewhere.
On this occasion, Jakub Frank's skull was removed from his grave and, carefully labeled as "the skull of a Jewish patriarch", ended up in the hands of Offenbach's historian.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances, it ended up in Berlin, where it underwent detailed measurements and studies and deemed an example of Jewish racial inferiority.
After the war, it disappeared without a trace possibly destroyed by wartime chaos disintegrated into dust or could still lie in underground storage facilities of some museum.
After Jakub's death, a time of great peace began for me.
My main occupation became studying the Merkavah, and then also our conversations with Jeruchim Dembowski, as we lived in one room and got closer to each other.
I told him, Jeruchim, about Chai Szor who was the only woman I could love and did love from that beautiful moment when I had her for one night when I came with news about Jakub to Rohatyn.
But above all else, I loved Jakub.
They had been in Ivanye since April.
If it weren't for the kind people of Ivanye, they would have likely starved to death.
Ivanye saved their lives and health, Bejla was feeling better now and didn't cough as much.
Srol believes that once they are baptized, they will be living as well as the Christians.
They will get a piece of land, Bejla will have vegetables in her garden and he, Srol, will weave rugs because he is good at it.
In their old age when their daughters are married off, they'll be taken in by them.
These are all his dreams.
"Look here, benefactor," Roszko says grimly as the carriage stops.
"Kashka doesn't want to go.
Roszko steps down from his perch and gesticulates a farewell several times.
Then he leans over and peers into the fog as though gazing into water.
His festive red, albeit somewhat faded, coat reveals a shirt underneath.
"I don't know where to go," he says.
"What do you mean you don't know?
We are already on the Rohatyn highway," says the surprised priest.
Even so!
He gets out of the carriage and follows his servant helplessly around it, straining his eyes into the white haze.
They think they see something but their eyes making up tricks when they can't focus on anything.
Could anything like this have happened to them?
It's as if they'd lost themselves in their own pocket!
"Quiet!"
The priest suddenly raises his finger overhead, listening intently And indeed, from somewhere on their left side above the mist comes a faint sound of water flowing:
"Let's follow that noise," he decides after a moment's pause.
That's water flowing.
Soon the priest relaxes in his carriage, stretches out his legs, and lets his eyes roam over a sea of fog.
Instantly he falls into travel thoughtfulness, as people think best when in motion.

Slowly and hesitantly, the mechanism of his mind comes to life, gears and wheels start turning, setting the driving wheels in motion just like in the clock that stands on the parsonage hallway at home; it was expensive having been bought in Lviv.
Any moment now it will chime.
He begins to wonder if anything exists beneath such fog at all?
After all Jewish historian Josephus Flavius maintained that the world was created during autumn equinox.
It's a feasible theory because there were fruits in paradise; given that an apple hung from a tree it must have been autumn.
There is some sense in this reasoning.
However he immediately thinks:
What kind of argument is this?
Could not the Almighty God create insignificant fruits miraculously at any time of year?
As they reach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they join a stream of pedestrians, riders, and carts of all kinds that emerge from the fog, like little bread figures made for Christmas.
It's Wednesday, market day in Rohatyn; there are peasant carts loaded with sacks of grain, cages full of poultry and all sorts of agricultural produce.
Alongside them briskly march traders carrying on their backs every possible goods their stalls cunningly folded up now as though on a yoke.
In a moment they will unfold into tables overflowing with colorful materials and wooden toys or eggs bought in villages at one-fourth their price.
The peasants also lead goats and cows intended for sale; the terrified animals baulk at each puddle with all the noise around them.
A speedy wagon covered with a leaky tarpaulin filled with rowdy Jews passes by; they have descended onto Rohatyn's market from all surrounding areas.

Then a wealthy carriage struggles through behind them its bright lacquered door is muddy black due to crowd's sludge and fog making it difficult to keep its dignity intact   from within which emanate expressions that suggest discomfort on an upper servant's face wrapped under blue cloak.
Clearly unprepared for such pandemonium he desperately scans his surroundings for an opportunity to break away from this cursed road.
